title: Olathe Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Olathe wells have a 35-foot median depth; see yields, water levels, drilling costs, permit history, and risks before buying.
h1: Olathe Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
If you are buying land or a home near Olathe, the nearby well records point to generally shallow wells, but not every parcel follows that pattern. Within five miles, Colorado DWR records include 214 permitted wells, with 109 recorded as constructed. The median reported depth is 35 feet, while the deepest record reaches 933 feet. That spread matters when you price a new well: a shallow alluvial well may be straightforward, but a difficult site can require a much deeper hole.

This page uses permitted-well records around Olathe in Montrose County. Treat the numbers as local evidence, not a guarantee for one lot. A driller still needs to evaluate access, geology, casing and grout requirements, water quality, septic layout, and the intended household or irrigation use.

sections.heading: Olathe well depths: shallow locally, with exceptions
sections.html:
Olathe’s reported well depth is 35 feet at the median, and the middle half of records falls between 21 and 71 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling estimate because 76% of the reported depth records are under 100 feet. Still, the local range is wide: 7% are 100 to 300 feet, 11% are 300 to 600 feet, and 5% are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record is 933 feet.

The permits mostly identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 210 wells in that category. Two name the Mancos, and one names the Morrison. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can change quickly across a property. Ask a driller to compare nearby logs, not just use the 35-foot median when preparing a bid.

sections.heading: What Olathe wells produce
sections.html:
Only five wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics are based on a small sample. Among those reports, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Eighty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 20% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. No reported wells fall under 1 gallon per minute or in the 1 to 5 gallon-per-minute range.

That looks favorable, but it is not a promise for an untested lot. A driller’s test and a properly sized pump, pressure tank, and storage system matter more than a map summary. Confirm the permitted use as well: the local records include domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, and those uses do not all represent household supply performance.

sections.heading: Water levels near Olathe and what the records show
sections.html:
The five reported static water levels have a median depth to water of 32 feet, with the middle half between 14 and 37 feet. For a buyer, that suggests water may be encountered relatively close to the surface in some parts of the area, but it should not be read as the expected drilling depth. A well can pass through shallow water-bearing material and still require different construction for dependable production.

The available water-level sample is too small to establish a reliable long-term decline or rise. The permit history shows wells from the 1950s through the 2020s, with the newest permit issued in 2025, but that does not create a decade-by-decade water-table trend. Request the well log, static level, pumping test, and recent water-quality results for the specific property.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Olathe, and when
sections.html:
The permit record is spread across many decades, with 11 permits in the 1950s, 5 in the 1960s, 15 in the 1970s, 9 in the 1980s, 23 in the 1990s, 22 in the 2000s, 47 in the 2010s, and 4 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. More recent activity gives you additional nearby logs to compare, while older wells can still show how ground conditions vary across the valley and nearby uplands.

The most active driller listed is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 35 records. K. W. Anderson Drilling, recorded as Anderson, Kermit W, has 11, and Johnson Brothers, recorded as Johnson, Chester T, has 7. These are permit-record names, not recommendations. Verify current licensing, insurance, references, access requirements, and the proposed well construction before hiring.

sections.heading: What a new Olathe well may cost
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in this area, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $1,800 to $2,600. That is only the drilling portion, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $7,800 to $14,600 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, testing, treatment, or a longer utility run can move the final bid higher. Ask for a written breakdown separating drilling, casing, grout, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, permits, and testing so competing bids describe the same work.

sections.heading: Olathe risks to check before you commit
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The records include a small yield sample, and the depth range runs from shallow wells to 933 feet, so a dry hole or a costly deeper well remains a site-specific possibility. Fractured-bedrock conditions can be unpredictable even where neighboring wells perform well. Have the driller review nearby logs and explain the stopping, casing, and testing plan before work starts.

Water quality also deserves attention. Within about ten miles, the mapped environmental information includes 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, one historic mine feature, and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site. That does not prove a problem on your property, but it supports testing for the contaminants relevant to the site. Keep the well, septic system, and future building area separated as required, and confirm that the lot can meet Colorado septic and setback requirements.

sections.heading: Buying or building on an Olathe lot
sections.html:
Before closing, obtain the DWR permit, well construction report, pump information, water-quality results, and any recorded production or static-level data. Compare the property with nearby wells in Olathe and the surrounding areas, including Delta, Montrose, Orchard City, Lazear, Hotchkiss, and Cedaredge. Local comparison is more useful than relying on a countywide assumption.

If you plan to build, check the water right and permitted use early. An exempt household-use well has limits, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and an over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan. Confirm the intended domestic, stock, irrigation, or other use with Colorado DWR. Price access for a drill rig, power, trenching, septic, and construction equipment before making the offer.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Olathe, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within five miles of Olathe is 35 feet, and the middle half runs from 21 to 71 feet. About 76% of reported wells are under 100 feet. The range is still wide: the deepest record is 933 feet, so nearby records should guide a site-specific estimate rather than a median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Olathe?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot for mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 35-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $1,800 to $2,600. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $7,800 to $14,600, before unusual access, treatment, or deeper drilling costs.

faq.q: How much water do Olathe wells produce?
faq.a: Only five nearby records report a pump yield, so the sample is limited. The reported median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is also 15.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Eighty percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 20% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. A test is still necessary for a specific lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Olathe?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from the permit map alone. The area has 17 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about ten miles, along with one historic mine feature and one EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the individual well, especially before drinking the water, and review construction, septic separation, and nearby land uses.

faq.q: Are Olathe wells running dry or losing water?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a dependable water-table trend. Only five wells report static water levels; their median depth to water is 32 feet, with a middle half of 14 to 37 feet. The permit history reaches from the 1950s to a newest permit in 2025, but that is not enough by itself to show a long-term decline.
